summary: House rules the repository owner set in his own words while reviewing client work built with OpenDesigner (2026-11-03 and 2026-11-02). Two concern colour and apply to every project: colours with a meaning people already know keep that colour, and a product never uses pure white and pure black together. They are recorded here so they can become house standards with a source, like rules from the other non-negotiable sources.
key_ideas: Colours with a commonly known meaning keep it across every project unless the person asks otherwise: approved green, rejected red, pending amber, info blue; a well-known app keeps its own colour.
Using the known colours makes an interface feel familiar and less machine-made.
A product that uses pure white (#FFFFFF) does not also use pure black (#000000), and the reverse.
Per-project colour choices such as one client's neutrals are not house rules.

entities.name: Kunal (Billu)
entities.description: The OpenDesigner repository owner, who set these rules.

claims: Commonly used colours are recognised by people and make an application feel less AI-made.
Mixing pure white and pure black brings issues later.
quotes: keep that consistency in things across whatever projects we are working
if somebody is using absolute white, then they should not use absolute black

rules.rule: Keep the commonly known colour for a meaning: approved or success green, rejected or error red, pending or warning amber, info blue; a well-known app or channel keeps its own colour (Microsoft Teams purple, email in Outlook blue, a call green). The brand accent never takes a meaning that has a known colour.
rules.why: People recognise the known colours at a glance, and they make the product feel made with care, not by AI.

rules.rule: If a product uses pure white (#FFFFFF), it does not use pure black (#000000), and if it uses pure black it does not use pure white. Use an off-black such as #111111 with pure white, or an off-white with pure black.
rules.why: The owner's rule for every project: the two extremes together are harsh and cause problems later.

examples: A landing page showed a red brand button beside a red 'rejected' state and Teams in orange; the owner asked for the known colours across every project.
caveats: The neutrals #FFFFFF with #111111 were that one project's choice, not a default for everyone (owner, 2026-11-02).
